To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
systemic deficits in TAP‐1 or protease LMP2 have no effect on tumor development.
the absence of TAP or LMP2 does not alter the relative incidence of lymphoma vs. sarcoma in p53–/− mice.
(1) T cells can attack tumors; (2) T cells can kill some tumor cells; and (3) T cells are not able to limit tumorigenisis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the immune system in the development and progression of cancer.
the role of the T‐cell response in tumorigenesis.
understanding the mechanisms of tumor escape from T‐cell surveillance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the absence of TAP‐1 or proteosomal subunit LMP‐2 does not affect the development and progression of tumors in the absence of functional p53, but it is possible that a small number of tumor types might be affected by these deficiencies.
the immune system does not play a significant role in the prevention of cancer, but rather it plays a role in the elimination of cancer cells after they have developed.
the TAP‐1 and LMP‐2 gene products are not rate‐limiting factors in the development of tumors in the p53‐defective mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the TAP1–LMP2 pathway does not play a significant role in tumor immunity.
we have shown that the absence of TAP or LMP2 does not alter the rate of tumor development in p53‐defective mice.
TAP1 and proteasome LMP2 have no major impact on tumorigenesis, and T cells do not exert a major impact on tumour incidence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T cells are not effective at preventing tumor formation, even though some tumors can be killed by T cells.
systemic deficits in TAP or proteasome components did not alter the incidence or types of spontaneous tumors in mice.
T‐cells do not appear to be a significant barrier to the development of cancer.
